modules.title: Unit 2 — Olá, tudo bem? Greetings, personal data and introductions
modules.description: Greet people, introduce yourself formally and informally, give personal data on forms, talk about countries, nationalities and numbers.

topics.title: Greetings, introductions and forms of address
topics.context:
Use these phrases every day in Portugal: when you greet people, introduce yourself, and speak politely in class, at work, or at a service desk. With friends, classmates and children, use **tu**: **Como te chamas?** With staff, teachers and older adults, use 3rd-person forms, often with **o senhor / a senhora**: **Como se chama?**

Examples:
- **Olá!** — *Hello!*
- **Bom dia. Chamo-me Raj.** — *Good morning. My name is Raj.*
- **Ela chama-se Oksana.** — *Her name is Oksana.*
- **Sou nepalesa. Tenho vinte anos.** — *I am Nepalese. I am twenty years old.*
- **Estou bem, obrigada.** — *I am well, thank you.*
- **Falas português? — Sim, um pouco.** — *Do you speak Portuguese? — Yes, a little.*
- **Muito prazer.** — *Nice to meet you.*
- **Com licença / Por favor / Obrigado(a).** — *Excuse me / Please / Thank you.*

Watch out:
- In statements with **chamar-se**, the pronoun goes after the verb: **Chamo-me Ana**, not **Me chamo Ana**.
- Greetings depend on the time: **Bom dia**, **Boa tarde**, **Boa noite**.

exercises.prompt: Ask your male teacher (formal) if he speaks Portuguese.

exercises.prompt: Your new classmate answers: «Sim, um pouco.» Ask him (informal) if he speaks Portuguese.

topics.title: Personal data and filling in forms
topics.context:
In Portugal, many forms at **AIMA**, **Finanças**, the **Centro de Saúde** or the **Loja do Cidadão** ask for the same personal data. Learn the field names and the ready-made questions officials use.

- **Nome**: *O meu nome é Raj.* — My first name is Raj.
- **Apelido**: *O meu apelido é Khan.* — My surname is Khan.
- **Data de nascimento**: *A minha data de nascimento é 12/05/1990.* — My date of birth is 12/05/1990.
- **Nacionalidade / naturalidade**: *Sou nepalesa. A minha naturalidade é Catmandu.* — I am Nepalese. My place of birth is Kathmandu.
- **Morada / código postal / localidade**: *A minha morada é Rua Nova, 8.* — My address is Rua Nova, 8.
- Officials ask: *Qual é o seu nome? Qual é a sua morada? Onde mora?* — What is your name? What is your address? Where do you live?
- With **-ar** verbs: *Moro em Faro. Trabalho numa loja. Falo português.* — I live in Faro. I work in a shop. I speak Portuguese.

**Watch out:** **NIF** and **NISS** are different numbers. Also, in European Portuguese, use the article with possessives: *o seu nome, a sua morada*.

keyItems.note: Número de Identificação da Segurança Social

exercises.explanation: To ask for a field on a form, use «Qual é a / o sua / seu ...?». «Nacionalidade» is feminine, so it takes «a sua».

exercises.explanation: For informal singular, use «a tua». The noun «profissão» is feminine: «Qual é a tua profissão?».

exercises.explanation: «Profissão» is feminine. In European Portuguese, use the article and the matching possessive: «a sua profissão».

exercises.explanation: For personal data, you can answer with a short sentence like «Sou solteiro/a», or say politely that you prefer not to answer.

topics.title: Countries, nationalities and languages
topics.context:
Use **ser de** to say where someone is from, and **ser** + nationality to say nationality. Use **falar** for languages.

- *Sou da Índia.* — I am from India.
- *Sou de Portugal.* — I am from Portugal.
- *O João é português.* — João is Portuguese.
- *A Sunita é indiana e fala hindi.* — Sunita is Indian and speaks Hindi.
- *Moro no Porto.* — I live in Porto.
- *Moro na Amadora.* — I live in Amadora.
- *De onde é que és?* — Where are you from?
- *Qual é a tua nacionalidade?* — What is your nationality?

Some country names take an article, so **de** and **em** contract: *do Brasil, da Ucrânia, no Porto, na Amadora*. But with *Portugal* we normally say *de Portugal*. Nationalities agree with gender: *brasileiro / brasileira*, *ucraniano / ucraniana*. **Watch out:** after *falar*, language names usually come with no article: *Falo português e inglês.* **Watch out:** do not say *em o Porto* or *de o Brasil*; use *no Porto* and *do Brasil*.

keyItems.note: Portugal normally has no article here

topics.title: Numbers 0–300: age, phone, prices, addresses
topics.context:
In Portugal, numbers are used daily for ages, phone numbers, prices, and addresses. Remember that **um** and **dois** change gender before feminine nouns: *um euro* / *uma mesa*, *dois euros* / *duas casas*. Hundreds also agree with gender: *duzentos euros* (masculine) vs. *duzentas pessoas* (feminine).

For 100, use **cem** when exact (*cem euros*), but **cento** when followed by another number (*cento e um*, *cento e vinte*).

Examples:
- *Tenho trinta e dois anos.* (I am 32 years old.)
- *O meu número de telemóvel é 912 345 678.* (My mobile number is 912 345 678.)
- *Custa dois euros e cinquenta cêntimos.* (It costs two euros and fifty cents.)

modules.title: Unit 3 — O dia a dia: routine, family, time and plans
modules.description: Describe a daily routine with reflexive and regular -er/-ir verbs, talk about family, tell the time and dates, say what is happening now and future plans.

topics.title: Daily routine and reflexive verbs
topics.context:
Daily routine is very useful in Portugal: in class, at work, and in small talk, people often ask about times and habits. In this topic, you practise common routine verbs and a key grammar point: **reflexive pronouns**.

In a normal affirmative sentence, the pronoun usually goes **after** the verb with a hyphen:
- **Levanto-me às sete.** = I get up at seven.
- **Deito-me tarde.** = I go to bed late.

After words like **não**, **nunca**, **também** and after **question words**, the pronoun goes **before** the verb:
- **Não me levanto cedo.** = I do not get up early.
- **Também me deito tarde.** = I also go to bed late.
- **A que horas te levantas?** = What time do you get up?

You also revise some regular **-er** and **-ir** verbs:
- **Vivo em Lisboa.** = I live in Lisbon.
- **Escreve emails de manhã.** = She writes emails in the morning.
- **Como pão ao pequeno-almoço.** = I eat bread for breakfast.

Watch out:
- **sempre** normally comes **after** the verb: **Janto sempre em casa.**
- **costumar** is followed directly by an infinitive: **Costumo jantar cedo.**

keyItems.support: I also go to bed late.

exercises.prompt: Say: I always get up at seven.
exercises.explanation: With reflexive verbs in an affirmative sentence, the pronoun goes after the verb with a hyphen: «levanto-me». In European Portuguese, «sempre» normally comes after the verb.
acceptedAnswers: Eu levanto-me sempre às sete.

exercises.prompt: Say that Raj does not get dressed early.
exercises.explanation: After «não», reflexive pronouns go before the verb: «não se veste». The verb is 3rd person singular with «Raj».
acceptedAnswers: Raj não se veste cedo.

exercises.prompt: Say: I usually have breakfast at home. Use «costumar + infinitive».
exercises.explanation: «Costumar» is followed directly by an infinitive: «costumo tomar». For meals at home, use «em casa».
acceptedAnswers: Eu costumo tomar o pequeno-almoço em casa.

exercises.prompt: Say that Sunita and Ahmed go to work (use «ir para»).
exercises.explanation: In Portugal first names usually take the article: «a Sunita», «o Ahmed». For a destination use «ir para»; two people → plural «vão».
acceptedAnswers: Sunita e Ahmed vão para o trabalho.

exercises.prompt: Say: I also go to bed late.
exercises.explanation: After «também», the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb: «também me deito». This is different from a simple affirmative sentence without a trigger word.
acceptedAnswers: Eu também me deito tarde.

exercises.prompt: Your friend answers: «Às seis e meia.» Ask her (informal) what time she wakes up.
exercises.explanation: Use «A que horas» for clock time. «Acordar» here is not reflexive, so the question is «acordas», not «te acordas».
acceptedAnswers: A que horas é que acordas?

exercises.prompt: Your classmate answers: «Tomo banho de manhã.» Ask him (informal) when he takes a shower.
exercises.explanation: Use «Quando» to ask about part of the day or another moment. «Tomar banho» is a fixed everyday expression.
acceptedAnswers: Quando é que tomas banho?

exercises.prompt: Your friend answers: «Não, nunca me deito tarde.» Ask her (informal) if she goes to bed late.
exercises.explanation: In a yes/no question, you can begin with the verb: «Deitas-te...?» In an affirmative question form, the reflexive pronoun stays after the verb.
acceptedAnswers: Tu deitas-te tarde?

exercises.prompt: Your classmate answers: «Vivo em Faro.» Ask him (informal) where he lives, using «viver».
exercises.explanation: Use «Onde» to ask where someone lives. With «tu», regular -er verbs end in «-es»: «vives».
acceptedAnswers: Onde é que vives?

exercises.prompt: A neighbour answers: «Deito-me às onze.» Ask her (formal) what time she goes to bed.
exercises.explanation: With formal «a senhora / você», the verb is 3rd person singular: «deita». After the question phrase, the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb: «se deita».
acceptedAnswers: A que horas é que se deita?
A que horas se deita a senhora?
A que horas é que a senhora se deita?

exercises.prompt: Say: I wake up at seven and then I get up straight away. Fill the two gaps.
exercises.explanation: «Acordar» is not reflexive here, but «levantar-se» is. In an affirmative sentence, the reflexive pronoun is attached after the verb: «levanto-me».
exercises.template: Eu ___ às sete e depois ___ logo.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gaps with the correct «tu» forms.
exercises.explanation: With «tu», regular -er and -ir verbs usually end in «-es»: «comes», «abres».
exercises.template: Tu ___ pão ao pequeno-almoço e ___ a janela do quarto.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence about Oksana.
exercises.explanation: For ela / a Oksana, regular -er and -ir verbs take 3rd person singular: «vive», «escreve», «decide».

exercises.prompt: Say: I don't go to bed early, but I always have breakfast at home. Fill the gaps.
exercises.explanation: After «não», the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb: «não me deito». «Sempre» normally comes after the verb: «tomo sempre».
exercises.template: Não ___ cedo, mas ___ sempre o pequeno-almoço em casa.

exercises.prompt: One word is wrong. Tap it and choose the correction.
exercises.explanation: With «tu», the verb needs the ending «-as»: «levantas-te». «Levanta-se» would be for ele, ela, o senhor or a senhora.

exercises.prompt: One word is wrong. Tap it and choose the correction.
exercises.explanation: After «nunca», the pronoun goes before the verb, so the correct pattern is «nunca te deitas». Do not keep an extra «-te» on the verb.

exercises.prompt: One word is wrong. Tap it and choose the correction.
exercises.explanation: With «os comboios» (they), the present form of «partir» is «partem». «Parte» is singular.

exercises.explanation: «Deitar-se» is reflexive. In a normal affirmative sentence with «eu», the pronoun is attached after the verb: «deito-me».

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: For «they», regular -er verbs usually end in «-em»: «escrevem».

exercises.explanation: Use a time after «A que horas». With «levantar-se», keep the reflexive form: «levanto-me».

exercises.sampleAnswer: Levanto-me às sete nos dias de trabalho.

exercises.prompt: Say: I never get up at six on Sundays.
exercises.explanation: With «nunca», the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb: «me levanto». For repeated days, Portuguese often uses «aos domingos».
acceptedAnswers: Eu nunca me levanto às seis aos domingos.

exercises.prompt: Say: We usually have lunch at one.
exercises.explanation: «Costumar» is followed by an infinitive, not a conjugated verb. With «nós», the verb is «costumamos».

exercises.prompt: Your classmate answers: «Levanto-me às seis e meia.» Ask him (informal) at what time he gets up.
exercises.explanation: After «A que horas», the reflexive pronoun goes before the verb: «te levantas». In Portugal, the version with «é que» is also very common.

exercises.prompt: Your friend answers: «Costumo jantar às sete e meia.» Ask him (informal) at what time he usually has dinner.

acceptedAnswers: A que horas é que costumas jantar?

exercises.prompt: A woman at work answers: «Almoço ao meio-dia.» Ask her (formal) at what time she has lunch.
exercises.explanation: For formal singular, Portuguese uses the 3rd-person verb form: «almoça». «A que horas» asks for the exact time.
acceptedAnswers: A que horas é que almoça?
A que horas almoça a senhora?
A que horas é que a senhora almoça?

exercises.explanation: In an affirmative sentence, the reflexive pronoun goes after the verb with a hyphen: «levantamo-nos». «Tomar banho» is a fixed everyday expression.
exercises.template: Ao sábado, nós ___ tarde e depois ___ banho em casa.

exercises.prompt: Say: Li never gets dressed quickly, and I also get dressed slowly. Fill the two gaps.
exercises.explanation: After «nunca» and «também», the reflexive pronoun comes before the verb: «se veste», «me visto». This is different from normal affirmative sentences like «visto-me».
exercises.template: A Li ___ depressa e eu ___ devagar.

exercises.prompt: One word is wrong. Tap it and choose the correction.
exercises.explanation: After «costumo», Portuguese uses an infinitive: «costumo jantar». A conjugated form like «janto» does not fit here.

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: «Abrir» is a regular -ir verb. For «eu», the form is «abro».
exercises.sentence: I **open** the shop at nine every day.

exercises.prompt: Answer about yourself.
exercises.explanation: Use the present tense to talk about your daily routine. «A que horas» is the normal way to ask about the time of a habit.

exercises.sampleAnswer: Almoço ao meio-dia.

topics.title: Family and possessives
topics.context:
In this topic you learn family words and two very common ways to show possession. In European Portuguese, a possessive before a noun normally comes with the definite article: **o meu pai**, **a tua irmã**, **os nossos avós**. You use these forms when you talk about relatives, children and family members. You also learn **dele / dela / deles / delas** after the noun: **a casa deles**, **o carro dela**.

Examples:
- **A minha mãe mora em Braga.** — My mother lives in Braga.
- **O teu irmão trabalha no hospital?** — Does your brother work at the hospital?
- **Os nossos avós vivem em Faro.** — Our grandparents live in Faro.
- **A sua filha chama-se Inês.** — Your daughter is called Inês. / His or her daughter is called Inês.
- **Tenho dois filhos.** — I have two children / two sons, depending on the context.
- **A casa deles é pequena.** — Their house is small.
- **Quantos irmãos tem?** — How many brothers and sisters do you have? (formal)

Watch out:
- In Portugal, do not drop the article before a possessive noun: say **a minha mãe**, not **minha mãe**.
- After the noun, use **dele / dela / deles / delas**: **o filho dela**, **a casa deles**.

keyItems.note: used before a noun with an article
used after the noun or after «ser»

keyItems.support: I have two children / two sons.

keyItems.target: Quantos irmãos tens? / Quantos irmãos tem?
keyItems.support: How many brothers and sisters do you have?

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: Family words have fixed forms. «Mãe» means «mother».
exercises.sentence: My **mother** lives in Coimbra.

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: «Irmão» is the masculine form for «brother». «Irmã» is «sister».
exercises.sentence: João has one **brother** and two sisters.

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: «Marido» means «husband». For «wife», Portuguese often uses «mulher» or «esposa».
exercises.sentence: Her **husband** works at the hospital.

exercises.prompt: Match the family words with their meanings.
exercises.explanation: Some family words change by gender and number, for example «cunhado / cunhada» and «netos / netas».

exercises.prompt: Ahmed is talking about his children. Fill the two gaps.
exercises.explanation: After «dois» you need a masculine plural noun, and after «uma» you need a feminine singular noun.
exercises.template: O Ahmed tem dois ___ e uma ___.

exercises.prompt: You are talking about your own parents. Complete with the right possessive. The article is already there.
exercises.explanation: In European Portuguese, the possessive comes after the article and agrees with the noun: «a minha mãe», «o meu pai».
exercises.template: A ___ mãe mora em Aveiro e o ___ pai trabalha no Porto.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking formally to a woman about her family. Complete the sentence.
exercises.explanation: With formal singular, Portuguese uses the 3rd-person possessives «seu / sua». They still agree with the noun.
exercises.template: A ___ filha chama-se Inês e o ___ marido chama-se Raj.

exercises.prompt: Complete: the house belongs to them (men or a mixed group), and the car belongs to her.
exercises.explanation: After the noun or after «ser», use «dele / dela / deles / delas» to show possession.
exercises.template: A casa é ___ e o carro é ___.

exercises.prompt: Say, while showing a photo: This is my mother.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, European Portuguese normally uses the article with the possessive: «a minha mãe».
acceptedAnswers: É a minha mãe.
Ela é a minha mãe.

exercises.prompt: Say that Raj has two sons.
exercises.explanation: Use «tem» for «has». After «dois», the noun is plural: «filhos».
acceptedAnswers: O Raj tem dois filhos.

exercises.prompt: Say: Our grandparents live in Faro.
exercises.explanation: The possessive and the noun are both plural here: «os nossos avós».
acceptedAnswers: Os nossos avós vivem em Faro.

exercises.prompt: Say: Their house (those men or a mixed group) is small.
exercises.explanation: When possession comes after the noun, use «deles» for «their» with a masculine or mixed plural group.

exercises.prompt: Say: João is my brother-in-law.
exercises.explanation: Use «cunhado» for «brother-in-law». With a noun, Portuguese normally keeps the article before the possessive: «o meu cunhado».
acceptedAnswers: João é o meu cunhado.

exercises.prompt: Say: Her son is ten years old.
exercises.explanation: Age uses «ter»: «tem dez anos». For possession after the noun, use «dela».
acceptedAnswers: O filho dela tem 10 anos.
O seu filho tem dez anos.

exercises.prompt: Your friend answers: «Tenho uma irmã e dois irmãos.» Ask him (informal) how many brothers and sisters he has. Use the common question with «irmãos».
exercises.explanation: In everyday Portuguese, «irmãos» can mean siblings in general. With «tu», the verb is «tens».
exercises.givenAnswer: Tenho uma irmã e dois irmãos.
acceptedAnswers: Quantos irmãos é que tens?

exercises.prompt: Your neighbour answers: «A minha irmã chama-se Mariana.» Ask him (formal) what his sister is called. Use «chamar-se».
exercises.explanation: In a formal question, keep the 3rd-person form: «se chama». The possessive still takes an article: «a sua irmã».
acceptedAnswers: Como é que se chama a sua irmã?
Como é que a sua irmã se chama?

exercises.prompt: Your friend answers: «O meu pai mora em Braga.» Ask her (informal) where her father lives. Use «morar».
exercises.explanation: Ask about place with «Onde». Keep European Portuguese order: question word + verb + subject.
exercises.givenAnswer: O meu pai mora em Braga.
acceptedAnswers: Onde é que mora o teu pai?
Onde é que o teu pai mora?

exercises.prompt: Pointing to a building, your classmate answers: «É a casa deles.» Ask informally whose house it is. Use exactly the words «a casa» in the question.
exercises.explanation: To ask about possession, use «De quem». You can also hear the emphatic pattern with «é que».
acceptedAnswers: De quem é que é a casa?

exercises.prompt: One word is wrong. Tap it and choose the correction.
exercises.explanation: The possessive must agree with the noun. «Mãe» is feminine, so we say «a minha mãe».

exercises.prompt: Answer about yourself.
exercises.explanation: You can answer with «Tenho...» and then add the family words you need.
exercises.question: Tens irmãos?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Tenho um irmão e uma irmã.

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: «Tio» is the masculine family word for an uncle. «Tia» is an aunt.
exercises.sentence: My **uncle** lives in Santarém.

exercises.prompt: Choose the Portuguese for the word in bold.
exercises.explanation: «Sogro» means father-in-law. It is a family relation by marriage.
exercises.sentence: Her **father-in-law** works near the station.

exercises.prompt: Raj is talking about his family. Fill the two gaps.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, Portuguese normally uses article + possessive. The form changes with the gender of the noun: «o seu tio», «a sua prima».
exercises.template: O Raj fala com ___ tio e com ___ prima ao domingo.

exercises.prompt: Mariana is presenting the family. Fill the three gaps.
exercises.explanation: Use article + possessive before the noun: «o meu irmão», «a sua mulher». After the noun, use «deles / delas»: «os filhos deles».
exercises.template: ___ irmão chama-se Tiago, ___ mulher é médica e os filhos ___ estudam no Porto.

exercises.prompt: Say: Our son studies in Porto.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, «nosso» needs the article in European Portuguese: «o nosso filho». «Porto» usually takes the article too: «no Porto».

exercises.prompt: Say about Raj and Ahmed: Their aunt is Brazilian.
exercises.explanation: After the noun, use «deles» for possession of Raj and Ahmed. The adjective agrees with «tia», so it is «brasileira».

exercises.prompt: Say to two friends: Your female cousins live in Braga.
exercises.explanation: For more than one person, use the plural possessive «as vossas». It agrees with the feminine plural noun «primas».
acceptedAnswers: As vossas primas vivem em Braga.

exercises.prompt: A couple answers: «Temos três filhos.» Ask them (plural) how many children they have.
exercises.explanation: To ask more than one person, use the plural verb «têm». «Quantos» is used with the masculine plural noun «filhos».
acceptedAnswers: Quantos filhos é que têm?

exercises.prompt: Mr Silva answers: «Sim, a minha esposa trabalha aqui.» Ask him (formal) if his wife, «a sua esposa», works here.
exercises.explanation: In the formal singular, use «a sua» + noun and the verb in the 3rd person: «trabalha».
exercises.givenAnswer: Sim, a minha esposa trabalha aqui.

topics.title: Time, days, months and time prepositions
topics.context:
In Portuguese, clock time usually uses **ser**: **É uma hora** but **São duas horas**. You can say **e meia** (half past), **e um quarto** (quarter past) and **menos dez** (ten to). Before a clock time, use **às**: **às oito**. With one o’clock, use **à**: **à uma**.

Days, months and time expressions are very useful for classes, work, appointments and transport. Use **na segunda-feira** for one specific Monday, but **à segunda-feira** for a habit or routine. With months, use **em**: **em maio**. For weekend, **no fim de semana** often means one weekend or a planned weekend, and **ao fim de semana** means a regular habit.

- **São quatro e meia.** — It is four thirty.
- **É meio-dia.** — It is noon.
- **A aula começa às oito e um quarto.** — The class starts at 8:15.
- **Tenho consulta na terça-feira.** — I have an appointment on Tuesday.
- **Trabalho à segunda-feira.** — I work on Mondays.
- **Faço compras ao fim de semana.** — I shop at weekends.

**Watch out**
- Days and months are normally written with lower-case letters: **segunda-feira, maio**.
- In these basic patterns, do not use **em** before a weekday: use **na terça-feira** or **à terça-feira**, depending on the meaning.

topics.title: What is happening now and future plans
topics.context:
Use two very common patterns in everyday Portuguese.

- **estar a + infinitive** = an action happening **now**.
- **ir + infinitive** = a **plan** or something you are going to do.

You also meet some important irregular present forms: **vou, vais, vai, vamos, vão**; **vejo / vês / vê / veem**; **leio / lês / lê / leem**; **saio / sais / sai**; **faço / fazes / faz**.

Examples:
- **Agora estou a aprender português.** — I am learning Portuguese now.
- **Neste momento, estamos a fazer o jantar.** — At this moment, we are making dinner.
- **Amanhã vou à Loja do Cidadão.** — Tomorrow I am going to the Citizens’ Shop.
- **Na próxima semana, vamos ver uma casa.** — Next week we are going to see a house.
- **No próximo ano, vai abrir uma loja.** — Next year he/she is going to open a shop.
- **Agora vocês veem o número no ecrã.** — You all see the number on the screen now.

**Watch out:** for actions happening now, use **estar a + infinitive**. For plans with **ir**, the next verb stays in the **infinitive**: **vou ver**, **vais sair**, **vamos fazer**.

topics.title: Food and shops
topics.context:
### Buying food in Portugal
In Portugal, different foods often belong to different shops or counters. Meat comes from the **talho**, fish and seafood from the **peixaria**, bread from the **padaria**, and ham or cheese from the **charcutaria**. In a **supermercado** or **mercado**, you often ask for quantities such as **um quilo de**, **meio quilo**, **uma dúzia**, **um pacote**, **uma lata** and **uma garrafa**.

Examples:
- **Queria meio quilo de queijo, por favor.** — “I’d like half a kilo of cheese, please.”
- **Quanto custa o quilo de salmão?** — “How much is the kilo of salmon?”
- **Na padaria, levo uma carcaça e uma broa.** — “At the bakery, I’m taking a bread roll and a corn loaf.”
- **Compro arroz, massa e iogurte no supermercado.** — “I buy rice, pasta and yogurt at the supermarket.”
- **Preciso de uma garrafa de azeite.** — “I need a bottle of olive oil.”
- **Onde compras carne? No talho.** — “Where do you buy meat? At the butcher’s.”

**Watch out:** after quantities, use **de**: **um quilo de frango**, **uma garrafa de azeite**. Also remember the shop names: **talho** is for meat, **peixaria** is for fish and seafood.

topics.title: At the restaurant and café
topics.context:
At cafés and restaurants in Portugal, you often need ready-made polite phrases more than long grammar. Learn the meal words **pequeno-almoço**, **almoço**, **lanche** and **jantar**, and menu words like **entrada**, **prato principal**, **acompanhamento**, **sobremesa**, **prato do dia**, **ementa** and **conta**. With staff, Portuguese often sounds softer with fixed chunks such as **Queria...**, **Podia...** and **Preferia...**. Learn these as whole phrases for now.

- «Queria uma mesa para duas pessoas.» — “I would like a table for two.”
- «Preferia perto da janela.» — “I would prefer to sit near the window.”
- «Para mim, uma dourada grelhada com batatas cozidas.» — “For me, a grilled sea bream with boiled potatoes.”
- «O que deseja?» — “What would you like?”
- «Mais alguma coisa?» — “Anything else?”
- «Podia trazer a conta, por favor?» — “Could you bring the bill, please?”

**Watch out:** in Portugal, the restaurant menu is usually **a ementa**. **Watch out:** cooking words agree with the noun: **peixe grelhado**, but **dourada grelhada** and **batatas cozidas**.

topics.title: Likes, preferences and modal verbs
topics.context:
Use these verbs to talk about tastes, choices and what you can, want or know how to do in everyday Portuguese.

- **Gosto de peixe.** = “I like fish.”
- **Gosto de cozinhar.** = “I like cooking.”
- **A Mariana adora café.** = “Mariana loves coffee.”
- **Prefiro peixe a carne.** = “I prefer fish to meat.”
- **Não gosto nada de picante.** = “I really don’t like spicy food.”
- **Posso trazer pão.** = “I can bring bread.”
- **Sei cozinhar arroz.** = “I know how to cook rice.”
- **Ponho pouco sal na sopa.** = “I don’t put much salt in the soup.”

**Watch out:** after **gostar**, keep **de**: **gosto de café**, not *gosto café*. With **preferir**, a statement compares two things with **a**: **Prefiro chá a café**. But a direct choice question normally uses **ou**: **Preferes chá ou café?**

Also remember these useful irregular present forms: **quero, posso, sei, trago, ponho**. In formal questions, use the 3rd-person form: **Prefere chá ou café?** / **Pode trazer água, por favor?**

keyItems.note: use de before a noun or infinitive

topics.title: Public services and documents
topics.context:
When you go to **Finanças**, **Segurança Social**, **AIMA** or the **Junta de Freguesia**, you often need a document, an appointment, and a ticket number. In Portugal, short ready-made phrases are very useful at the counter.

Examples:
- **Queria pedir o NIF.** — “I’d like to ask for a NIF.”
- **Preciso de um comprovativo de morada.** — “I need a proof of address.”
- **Tenho de marcar atendimento.** — “I have to make an appointment.”
- **O senhor tem de levar o passaporte.** — “You need to bring the passport.”
- **Deve esperar a sua vez.** — “You should wait your turn.”
- **A sua senha é para o balcão 7.** — “Your ticket is for counter 7.”

**Watch out**
- After **precisar**, use **de**: **preciso de** um documento / **preciso de** marcar atendimento.
- With possessives in European Portuguese, use the article: **o meu passaporte**, **a sua vez**.
- Very common contractions are **do** (= de + o) and **ao** (= a + o).

topics.title: Bank, post office and other services
topics.context:
At the bank, at **CTT** and in other everyday services, short ready-made phrases help a lot. You usually say what you want, what you need, or what document you have. Staff often answer with short instructions.

- **Queria abrir uma conta.** — *I would like to open an account.*
- **Tem de trazer o passaporte e o NIF.** — *You have to bring your passport and tax number.*
- **Quero levantar dinheiro no multibanco.** — *I want to withdraw cash at the cash machine.*
- **Preciso do meu IBAN para fazer uma transferência.** — *I need my IBAN to make a transfer.*
- **Queria enviar esta carta registada.** — *I would like to send this registered letter.*
- **Tenho um aviso para levantar uma encomenda.** — *I have a notice to collect a parcel.*
- **Na farmácia, preciso de um medicamento.** — *At the pharmacy, I need some medicine.*
- **Queria vinte euros de gasóleo, por favor.** — *I’d like twenty euros of diesel, please.*

**Watch out:** in Portugal people normally say **levantar dinheiro** and **cartão multibanco**.

**Watch out:** staff often use **tem de + infinitive** for instructions: **Tem de trazer o passaporte e o NIF.** Learn this as a useful chunk.

topics.title: Directions, imperative and public transport
topics.context:
Giving directions in Portugal requires choosing between formal (*o senhor / a senhora*) and informal (*tu*) imperative forms.

**Formal imperative (polite / strangers / service desks):**
- *Siga em frente.* (Go straight ahead.)
- *Vire à direita / à esquerda.* (Turn right / left.)
- *Atravesse a rua na passadeira.* (Cross the street at the zebra crossing.)
- *Apanhe o autocarro vinte e oito.* (Take bus 28.)
- *Saia na estação do Rossio.* (Get off at Rossio station.)
- *Espere na paragem.* (Wait at the bus stop.)
- *Venha por aqui.* (Come this way.)
- *Traga o seu passe.* (Bring your pass.)

**Informal imperative (friends / family / colleagues):**
- *Segue em frente.* (Go straight ahead.)
- *Vira à direita.* (Turn right.)
- *Atravessa a rua.* (Cross the street.)
- *Apanha o metro.* (Take the metro.)
- *Sai no Martim Moniz.* (Get off at Martim Moniz.)
- *Espera aqui.* (Wait here.)
- *Vem comigo.* (Come with me.)
- *Traz o bilhete.* (Bring the ticket.)

**Movement Prepositions:**
- **para**: direction / destination (*Vou para casa.*)
- **por / pelo / pela**: passage through a place (*Passo pela praça.*)
- **a / ao / à**: movement to a point (*Vou à estação de metro.*)

*Watch out:* In European Portuguese, formal imperatives use forms like *siga*, *vire*, *saia*, whereas informal imperatives use *segue*, *vira*, *sai*. Always use polite forms with officials, doctors, and strangers on the street!

topics.title: Invitations and arranging to meet
topics.context:
In this topic you learn useful chunks for inviting someone, answering an invitation, arranging a time and place, and talking about formal appointments. These are very practical phrases for life in Portugal with friends, classmates, neighbours and at service desks.

- «Queres ir tomar um café?» = “Do you want to go for a coffee?”
- «Vamos ao cinema no sábado?» = “Shall we go to the cinema on Saturday?”
- «Sim, vamos!» / «Boa ideia!» = “Yes, let’s go!” / “Good idea!”
- «Desculpa, não posso. Tenho de trabalhar.» = “Sorry, I can’t. I have to work.”
- «A que horas nos encontramos?» = “What time do we meet?”
- «Onde é que nos encontramos?» = “Where do we meet?”
- «Tenho uma marcação às dez.» = “I have an appointment at ten.”
- «Queria marcar para amanhã.» = “I would like to book for tomorrow.”

**Watch out:**
- Learn «Queria...» and «Pode ser...?» as polite ready-made chunks. You do not need new grammar yet.
- Notice the contractions: «ao cinema», «na estação», «às seis», «da estação».
